pass_a_gloss: according to its not being easy for outsiders to receive it), and wrath as anger beginning. Scripture seems in very many places to know a difference of wrath and anger, as also in Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath nor discipline me in your anger. But we do not define in the same way the rebuking wrath of God and the wrath that must be taken from us, nor the disciplining anger of the Lord and our own. For the things about God are said more tropically, while the things named about us are confessed passions and sins. The name of bitterness also lies in Jeremiah: and your bitterness, he says, rose up before me. I think then bitterness is now said by the apostle as we call some bitter, opposite to the sweet, for custom also knows sweet people and bitter; wrath as the anger beginning to come about in the soul upon someone; and anger perhaps not the genus of these and other like things, but that already ready and active toward punishment of the one thought to have wronged. And as a rule clamor also follows these passions, those who are bitter and wrathful and angry crying out and speaking more noisily and bringing forth words of bitterness and wrath and anger. Therefore besides the former things one must also practice that clamor be taken from us. And I think blasphemy which he commands to be taken from us is what those angered from passions often bring forth who even dare to speak against the divine in the time of anger, when every accusation about anything whatever is taken again in blasphemy; for those are said to blaspheme who speak evil of those of whom they speak evil. Therefore following the things about bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor it is said that one must also put away blasphemy. If indeed we also rank blasphemy upon every voice that speaks the divine badly, not only from grief and anger in times of displeasure when people speak ill but often also from ignorance of the word about truth, as is clear from the doctrines among the heterodox, then the one who declares the true word false or the false true also blasphemes, and especially about God and the things of God. Who then is so approved a money-changer as to know how to test all things and hold the good and abstain from every form of evil? And since some think anger sometimes arises reasonably, not well adding without cause to the gospel saying whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to the judgment—for some read whoever is angry with his brother without cause—let us shame them from the present saying that lets all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be taken from you. For clearly here the word all is said in common over all, so that no bitterness is conceded nor any wrath permitted nor any anger reasonably accompanying. And in the thirty-sixth Psalm, as all anger being sin (and likewise wrath), it is said cease from anger and forsake wrath. Therefore it is never reasonable to be angry with anyone. And not only must one labor that all bitterness and all wrath and all anger and all blasphemy be taken from us, but these with all malice; and we take malice either as the habit opposite to virtue or as wickedness. Become kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving yourselves as also God in Christ forgave us. We named the opposite of bitter sweet; but Paul seems now to call kindness the opposite rank to bitterness, metaphorically from foods; so we can understand Become kind to one another instead of be approachable and in character sweet and gentle. This happens if, putting away the raw and merciless and unsympathetic toward the neighbor, we become tenderhearted toward all, by these things granting the greatest gifts not only to those near but also to ourselves. Forgiving yourselves is other than forgiving one another, since whatever we do well in benefiting others, these things both because of the end and because of our being under the law are referred more to us than to those we seem to have done well. And we grant these things to ourselves which also God granted us in Christ, as receiving them and keeping them and imitating the one who granted and his manner of granting. But another, thinking forgiving yourselves differs in nothing from forgiving—
pass_b_english: —hard for outsiders to accept)—and they call wrath anger as it begins. Scripture often marks a difference between wrath and anger, as in "Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger." We do not define God's rebuking wrath the same way as the wrath we must cast off, nor the Lord's disciplining anger the same as ours. Speech about God is more figurative; what is named in us is plainly passion and sin.

Bitterness also appears in Jeremiah: "Your bitterness rose up before me." In Paul I take bitterness as we call people bitter rather than sweet—custom knows both. Wrath is anger starting in the soul toward someone. Anger here is not merely the genus of such feelings, but anger already primed and active to punish the one thought to have done wrong. Clamor usually rides with them: the bitter, wrathful, and angry shout and speak more noisily, pouring out words of bitterness, wrath, and anger. So clamor too must be practiced away.

Blasphemy to be removed is, I think, what the angry often utter when, from passion, they even dare to speak against God—when every charge about anything is swept into blasphemy. People "blaspheme" when they speak evil of those they speak evil of. So after bitterness, wrath, anger, and clamor, blasphemy too must be put off.

If we also take blasphemy as every voice that speaks badly of the divine—not only from grief and anger when people are displeased, but often from ignorance of the truth, as heterodox doctrines show—then whoever calls the true word false or the false true also blasphemes, especially about God and God's matters. Who is so approved a money-changer as to test all things, hold the good, and abstain from every form of evil?

Some think anger can be reasonable, and they insert "without cause" into the gospel saying that whoever is angry with his brother is liable to judgment. Shame them with this text: "Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be taken from you." Here "all" covers everything: no bitterness allowed, no wrath permitted, no anger excused as reasonable. Psalm 36 says, as if all anger (and wrath) were sin, "Cease from anger and forsake wrath." So it is never right to be angry with anyone. Labor to strip not only all bitterness, wrath, anger, and blasphemy, but these together with all malice—malice as the habit opposite virtue, or as wickedness.

[[Ephesians 4:32 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:32]] "Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving yourselves as God in Christ also forgave you." We called the opposite of bitter "sweet"; Paul names kindness as bitterness's opposite, by a food metaphor. So "be kind to one another" means be approachable, sweet in character, and gentle. That comes when we put off raw, merciless, unsympathetic ways toward the neighbor and become tenderhearted to all—and by that we grant the greatest gifts not only to others but to ourselves.

"Forgiving yourselves" is not the same as "forgiving one another." Whatever good we do in benefiting others returns more to us—by the end and by our being under the law—than to those we seem to help. We grant ourselves what God granted us in Christ when we receive it, keep it, and imitate the Giver and his way of giving. Another reader, thinking "forgiving yourselves" no different from "forgiving one another," continues in the next section.
